Clarity.justification: The paper is reasonably well-structured with clear hypothesis framing (H-E1 and H-M1) and tabulated results. The writing is generally understandable. However, several issues reduce clarity: (1) The paper's contribution is thin and could be communicated in a much shorter format. (2) The stratified baseline formula is introduced without sufficient motivation for why this particular decomposition is appropriate. (3) The term 'behavioral fingerprint' is used loosely—it essentially just means class-wise accuracy profiles, which is not a novel concept. (4) The discussion of the SmallCNN architecture reconstruction in the code (with extensive comments about spatial dimension mismatches and the use of AdaptiveAvgPool2d as a workaround) raises concerns about whether the model architecture was correctly reconstructed, which is never discussed in the paper. (5) The mean accuracy of 18.7% is mentioned but not adequately contextualized—this is barely above random (10%) for CIFAR-10, which fundamentally affects the interpretation of all results.

Novelty.justification: The paper presents very limited novelty. The 'existence' finding (H-E1)—that models with the same overall accuracy have different per-class performance—is essentially trivial and well-known in the machine learning community. Any practitioner knows that aggregate accuracy masks class-level variation. The variance decomposition used is straightforward. The 'mechanism' test (H-M1) uses the most basic possible approach (per-layer scalar statistics with Ridge regression) and fails, which is not surprising given the simplicity of the features and the small sample size. The paper does not introduce any new method, architecture, or theoretical insight. The framing as 'behavioral fingerprints' adds terminology but not substance. Prior work by Unterthiner et al. already demonstrated weight statistics can predict accuracy; the extension to class-wise prediction is incremental and the negative result, while honest, does not advance the field.

Soundness.justification: Several methodological concerns undermine soundness: (1) The model architecture reconstruction is questionable. The code reveals extensive trial-and-error to match the FC layer dimensions, ultimately using AdaptiveAvgPool2d(3) as a hack to force 3x3 spatial output. This means the reconstructed models may not match the original architecture, potentially corrupting all inference results. The paper never acknowledges this issue. (2) The sample size of 193 models is very small, especially for the mechanism test with 25 features and only 39 test samples. The paper acknowledges this but still draws conclusions. (3) The mean accuracy of 18.7% (barely above random for 10-class classification) means most models are severely undertrained, making the 'behavioral fingerprint' finding less meaningful—the variance could simply reflect random initialization patterns rather than learned behavioral differences. (4) The residual ratio threshold of 0.05 is arbitrary and not justified. (5) The stratified baseline is a specific linear model; the high residual ratio could partly reflect nonlinear relationships between overall accuracy and class-wise accuracy rather than genuine 'behavioral' information. (6) The code shows the experiment had issues with downloading the dataset (extremely slow Zenodo downloads), and there's a PoC script that trains new models rather than using the actual model zoo, raising questions about which results are actually reported. The experimental results JSON confirms the 193-model run completed successfully, but the architecture reconstruction concern remains.

Significance.justification: The paper's contributions are minimal. The existence finding is unsurprising—it would be remarkable if all models with the same accuracy had identical class-wise performance. The mechanism finding is a negative result with the simplest possible approach, which provides little actionable insight. The paper's main value is as a 'call to action' for using learned representations for behavioral prediction, but this suggestion is already implicit in the weight-space learning literature. The experimental setup is too limited (single architecture, single dataset, 193 models, undertrained models) to draw generalizable conclusions. The paper does not demonstrate any practical application of the findings. For a workshop paper, the scope might be acceptable, but the contribution remains very thin even by workshop standards.

strengths: Clear hypothesis-driven experimental framework with explicit pass/fail criteria (H-E1 and H-M1)
Honest reporting of negative results (H-M1 failure) with thoughtful discussion of contributing factors
Reproducible experimental setup with code provided and specific dataset references
weaknesses: The existence finding (67.6% unexplained variance) is essentially trivial—class-wise accuracy variation beyond aggregate accuracy is expected and well-known
The model architecture reconstruction is questionable (AdaptiveAvgPool2d hack to match dimensions), potentially invalidating all inference-based results, yet this is never discussed in the paper
Extremely small sample size (193 models, 39 test) with severely undertrained models (18.7% mean accuracy on CIFAR-10) limits the validity and generalizability of all conclusions
The mechanism test uses the simplest possible features (25 scalar statistics) with a linear model, making the negative result unsurprising and uninformative
No new methods, architectures, or theoretical insights are introduced—the paper is purely observational with limited scope
